power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

In total, seven participants were considered drop-outs (relapse: n=4; change in medication: n=2; other: n=1), and four participants were lost to follow-up as they either did not start the intervention or discontinued the training after one session (Fig. 1A).

Subjects were included if they were between 18 and 60 years of age, had approved relapsingremitting MS, an EDSS between 0 and 4, and approved sports suitability assessed by a medical doctor via an electrocardiogram (ECG) at rest and during exercise (custo diagnostic, custo med GmbH, Ottobrunn, Germany).

Subjects were excluded if they had any previous history of internal, cardiovascular or orthopedic disease that prohibit study participation, pregnancy or breastfeeding, and if they experienced a relapse or significant worsening of MS-related symptoms during the study period.

Participants were asked to arrive fasted and well hydrated, to avoid strenuous exercise (at least 48 hours) and to not drink alcohol, coffee or to take dietary supplements (at least 24 hours) prior to the visit.

Using concealed allocation, study participants were randomly assigned into the intervention or passive control group immediately after baseline testing using stratified permuted block randomization with a 1:1 allocation ratio and randomly varying block sizes of four and six.
After finishing the intervention phase, a four-week follow-up period was included into this study in which participants were asked to continue their daily life.
Furthermore, all participants were asked not to change their behavior in daily life routines such as exercise, nutrition, or sleep.
Healthy subjects were recruited through public announcements and carefully selected to match participants from the MS cohort for age, BMI and sex.

Subjects were included if they were between 18 and 60 years of age, had no internal, neurological or orthopedic diseases, no chronic intake of immunoregulatory or anti-inflammatory drugs, and no illness within four weeks before study participation.

The participants were asked to attend one visit at the sports medicine lab which included, similar to the assessment of the MS subjects, the collection of anthropometric data, a blood draw, and a CPET.
Written informed consent was obtained prior to participation.
Data from a total of 75 persons with MS and 29 matched healthy subjects were available for statistical analyses.
All subjects signed a written informed consent prior to participation.

text.text: Using multiparametric flow cytometry and state-of-the-art mass spectrometry, we demonstrate that exercise training promotes an anti-inflammatory state at both the systemic and immune-cell proteomic levels and ameliorates dysregulated CCR4 expression on disease-associated LFA-1α high CD4 + T cells in multiple sclerosis patients.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive neuroinflammatory autoimmune disease that primarily affects females, is commonly diagnosed in early adulthood, and affects more than 2.8 million people worldwide (1).
text.formatted: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive neuroinflammatory autoimmune disease that primarily affects females, is commonly diagnosed in early adulthood, and affects more than 2.8 million people worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Disease progression is driven by localized inflammatory processes within the central nervous system (CNS), leading to continuous neurodegeneration and diverse symptom complexes depending on affected CNS structures.

The main concept of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) is the modulation of peripheral immunity to mitigate inflammation-induced neurodegeneration either by preventing immune cell invasion into the CNS, (un-)targeted cell depletion, or dampening cellular activation (2, 3).
text.formatted: The main concept of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) is the modulation of peripheral immunity to mitigate inflammation-induced neurodegeneration either by preventing immune cell invasion into the CNS, (un-)targeted cell depletion, or dampening cellular activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3)</ref>.

text.text: Besides positive effects of regular exercise on patient-reported outcomes in MS(4), a growing body of evidence now supports the application of structured exercise programs to beneficially affect immune cell characteristics implicated in the immunopathology of the disease (5-7) without causing adverse effects, which are oftentimes a consequence of DMTs.

These observations are consistent with exerciseinduced anti-inflammatory effects in healthy subjects and other clinical populations (8, 9) and are complemented by increasing evidence that levels of physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), which are known to be decreased in persons with MS (10, 11), are associated with disease progression and neurodegeneration (12, 13).

text.text: Especially high-intensity interval training (HIIT) has been shown to be more effective in improving CRF both in healthy subjects and persons with MS (14, 15), but also regarding the modulation of disease-associated cellular and molecular disease markers (16, 17).

text.text: A main goal of drug therapies in MS is to dampen immune cell trafficking across or their attraction toward the blood-brain-barrier which is achieved by targeting adhesion molecules and chemokine receptors (18, 19).

text.text: Although preclinical studies report profound immunomodulatory effects of exercise on immune cell infiltration into CNS and lymphoid organs, cytokine production, and disease progression (20, 21), there is limited translational evidence for these findings (22).

text.text: Furthermore, most clinical studies investigating exercise-induced effects on the immune system in MS are limited by small sample sizes, short intervention periods, or targeted analytical approaches, which restrict the exploratory potential of resulting data.

Just recently, unbiased analyses of alterations within the proteome of circulating immune cells after one training session revealed profound intensity-dependent changes (23), providing implications of a significant remodeling of the cellular proteome with functional adaptions in the course of a training intervention over several months.

text.text: In this randomized controlled trial (RCT), we comprehensively investigated immediate and sustained effects of a three-month HIIT intervention on circulating immune cells in persons with MS and included a healthy control group matched for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI) for comparison.

We characterized MS-relevant T cell subsets and their expression of proteins involved in vascular adhesion and chemotaxis using flow cytometry and further assessed exercise-induced changes within the proteome of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) by mass spectrometry-based profiling of more than 7,000 proteins.

Besides a pronounced increase in physical fitness, HIIT induced immediate and sustained changes in composite indices of systemic inflammation, while changes within the PBMC proteome at follow-up indicated a shift of innate and adaptive immune cells toward anti-inflammatory phenotypes and a reduced abundance of proteins linked to chronic inflammatory disease (i.e., MTHFD2).

We further identified an LFA-1α high CD4 + T-cell subset that was associated with disease biomarkers and exhibited increased C-C chemokine receptor type 4 (CCR4) expression compared with healthy controls that declined in the intervention group.

Together, these findings advance our understanding of cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying exercise-induced immunomodulation in persons with MS, thereby strengthening the mechanistic basis for current recommendations of exercise and lifestyle physical activity.

Some limitations of this study should be addressed.

Based on the exploratory nature of including high dimensional data from untargeted proteomics and multiparametric flow cytometry, the majority of the results reported here were derived from exploratory analyses and should therefore be interpreted accordingly.
In addition, the generalizability of the present findings may be limited by the characteristics of the study cohort.

Although HIIT over three months was well tolerated and effective in our study cohort, this exercise regimen might not be equally applicable to persons with greater disease severity (EDSS > 4) due to more pronounced motor impairments.

text.text: Further, our access to biological samples was constrained to the peripheral blood compartment which limits clinically meaningful interpretation in this neuroinflammatory disease.
Future studies in this field should therefore acquire cerebrospinal fluid to better translate exercise-induced effects observed in the periphery to potential changes within the CNS.

Additionally, we did not perform functional assays in this study (e.g., transmigration assay across human brain endothelial cells, in-vitro stimulation assays using MS-specific autoantigens) which would provide mechanistic evidence for our observed findings.

Although we assessed exercise-induced changes of thousands of proteins within circulating PBMCs, they are composed of a heterogeneous mixture of adaptive and innate immune cells which mask the identification of cell type-specific alterations.
This limitation should be addressed in future studies by sorting cell types of interest such as CD4 + T cells and monocytes, thereby validating and extending our findings.

Another limitation that needs to be addressed is the heterogeneous use of MS-specific medications within the study cohort, which, although largely stable between groups over the study period, potentially introduced confounding effects.

In conclusion, we substantiate existing evidence on the beneficial effects of HIIT on physical fitness and systemic inflammation in persons with MS and significantly expand this knowledge by our findings on its ability to reshape cellular immunity toward antiinflammation on the phenotypic and proteomic level.

The finding that the strongest changes within the PBMC proteome emerged at follow-up is original and opens an interesting and overlooked perspective on delayed immunometabolic adaptations to training.

The observation of an exercise-induced decline in dysregulated CCR4 expression on disease-associated LFA-1α high CD4 + T cells proposes another potential mechanism of how exercise exerts immunomodulatory effects in MS.

Overall, our results strengthen national and international recommendations on regular exercise for persons with MS by providing biological underpinnings of exercise-induced immunomodulatory effects within the cellular immune system without causing any adverse effects.
A total of 75 persons with relapsing-remitting MS participated in this RCT.

Subjects were included if they were between 18 and 60 years of age, had approved relapsingremitting MS, an EDSS between 0 and 4, and approved sports suitability assessed by a medical doctor via an electrocardiogram (ECG) at rest and during exercise (custo diagnostic, custo med GmbH, Ottobrunn, Germany).
Study inclusion was further only considered if no adjustments in DMT were made within three months before study commencement.

Subjects were excluded if they had any previous history of internal, cardiovascular or orthopedic disease that prohibit study participation, pregnancy or breastfeeding, and if they experienced a relapse or significant worsening of MS-related symptoms during the study period.
If a change in DMT was made during the study period, respective time points were not considered for follow-up analysis.

The study was reviewed and approved by the ethics committee of the Leibniz Institute the first visit, written informed consent and disease-related data were obtained which was followed by baseline testing.
Each visit took place between 7 a.m. and 11 a.m. at the sports medical laboratory at TU Dortmund University.

Participants were asked to arrive fasted and well hydrated, to avoid strenuous exercise (at least 48 hours) and to not drink alcohol, coffee or to take dietary supplements (at least 24 hours) prior to the visit.
Questionnaires were filled out online using a link that was provided to the participants 24 hours before each testing day at the TU Dortmund University.

Each visit included the recording of anthropometric data, a blood draw, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) until voluntary exhaustion which was conducted on a cycle ergometer (Cortex Bike M) using the MetaLyzer 3B-R² (CORTEX Biophysik, Leipzig, Germany) during which heart rate was continuously measured

Using concealed allocation, study participants were randomly assigned into the intervention or passive control group immediately after baseline testing using stratified permuted block randomization with a 1:1 allocation ratio and randomly varying block sizes of four and six.
The random allocation sequence was computer-generated in Microsoft Excel by an investigator who was not involved in participant enrollment or assessments.
To ensure a balanced group allocation into each study arm, stratification factors were used and dichotomized as follows: age (18-34 vs. 35-60 years), EDSS (0-2.0 vs.
Due to the nature of the trial, participants could not be blinded to group allocation.

However, assessors taking outcome measures after the intervention phase and at follow-up were blinded to group allocation by avoiding any contact between participants and assessors throughout the study period (except for assessments).
The exercise intervention was conducted at the training facility at the TU Dortmund University.
Participants allocated to the HIIT group exercised three times per week over a three-month intervention period on a bicycle ergometer (ergoselect5, ergoline GmbH, Germany).
This intervention period was split into four blocks of three weeks with progressing intensity from block one to four.
The exercise intensity was determined by peak power output (PPO) in watts (W) that was achieved during the baseline assessment.

Each training session started with a five min warm-up, comprised a total of seven intervals of 90 seconds that were interspersed by active recovery periods of 3 min between each interval, and ended with a five min cool-down, resulting in a total training duration of 38,5 min.

Whereas the intensity during the active recovery phases remained constant over the entire study period (20-25% PPO), the exercise intensity progressively increased from block one to four (block 1: 70-75% PPO; block 2: 80-85% PPO; block 3: 85-90% PPO; block 4: >90% PPO).
text.formatted: Whereas the intensity during the active recovery phases remained constant over the entire study period (20-25% PPO), the exercise intensity progressively increased from block one to four (block 1: 70-75% PPO; block 2: 80-85% PPO; block 3: 85-90% PPO; block 4: >90% PPO).

text.text: Since the body adapts to the exercise stimulus over time, another CPET was conducted in intervention week six in order to update the PPO that was used for defining exercise intensity.
A detailed overview of the training intervention is provided in Supplementary Table S4.

text.text: During each training session, the heart rate was continuously measured (ers2 ECG Transmitter, ergoline GmbH, Germany) and the RPE (76) was quantified at training start, after the 4 th and the 7 th interval, respectively.

Severe adverse events, defined as i) severe cardiovascular, neurological, orthopedic, or pulmonary diseases (e.g. renal failure, hepatic dysfunction, cardiovascular disease) or ii) severe cardiovascular exacerbations, were recorded during the study period.
After finishing the intervention phase, a four-week follow-up period was included into this study in which participants were asked to continue their daily life.

For ethical reasons and to provide all participants the opportunity to benefit from the exercise program, the participants in the passive control group were included in a waiting list to be offered the same exercise program after the study period.
Furthermore, all participants were asked not to change their behavior in daily life routines such as exercise, nutrition, or sleep.

Participants attending less than 25 training sessions (corresponding to 70% of overall attendance) were considered non-compliant to the study protocol and were therefore excluded from follow-up analysis (6).

text.text: The CPET in week six was considered equivalent to a training session, since the conduction of three training sessions and a CPET within one week was not feasible.
Healthy subjects were recruited through public announcements and carefully selected to match participants from the MS cohort for age, BMI and sex.

Subjects were included if they were between 18 and 60 years of age, had no internal, neurological or orthopedic diseases, no chronic intake of immunoregulatory or anti-inflammatory drugs, and no illness within four weeks before study participation.

The participants were asked to attend one visit at the sports medicine lab which included, similar to the assessment of the MS subjects, the collection of anthropometric data, a blood draw, and a CPET.
The ramp protocol was chosen according to a recently published study by Wenzel et al. (78).

text.text: Questionnaires were filled out online using a link that was provided to the participants 24 hours before the testing day at the TU Dortmund University.
Written informed consent was obtained prior to participation.
Blood sampling was performed at each visit by vein puncture after the BIA when participants rested for ten min in a lying position.

PBMC purification was done immediately after blood draw from 27mL whole blood, collected in lithium heparin S-Monovettes ® (Sarstedt), by density gradient centrifugation at RT using SepMate™ PBMC Isolation Tubes (STEMCELL Technologies).
Purified PBMCs were resuspended in 1mL freezing medium (90% FBS, 10% DMSO), stored overnight in a cell freezing container at -80°C, and transferred to -150°C on the next day.
For serum isolation, Serum-Gel S-Monovettes ® (Sarstedt) were kept in upright position at 4-8°C for 30 min.
After clotting, tubes were centrifuged for 10 min at 2500xg at 4°C, aliquoted, and stored at -80°C until analysis.
The same sample preparation procedures were carried out for blood derived from the healthy control subjects.

Within 10 min after blood draw into lithium heparin S-Monovettes ® (Sarstedt), the absolute cell numbers of major blood cell populations were quantified on a Hematology Analyzer (SYSMEX XP3000, Norderstedt, Germany).
The SII was calculated as (platelets × neutrophils) × lymphocytes -1 and the NLR as neutrophils × lymphocytes -1.

Serum was used to measure both sNfL and sGFAP as RUO immunoassays (ECLIA, Electrochemiluminescence immunoassay, two-incubation step sandwich assay) according to the manufacturer's instructions using the Roche Cobas 8000 (Roche Elecsys ® module).
All laboratory technicians performing the analyses were blinded to the clinical data and group allocation.

Using Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS) from large reference databases (79, 80), z-scores from the quantified concentration of both parameters by adjusting for age and BMI (sNfL) or for age, BMI, and sex (sGFAP), respectively.

text.text: In brief, cryopreserved PBMCs were gently thawed in a water bath at 37°C, washed twice with PBS containing 1mM EDTA, and lysed in a commercial RIPA buffer containing 0.1% SDS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), 10mM sodium fluoride (Sigma-Aldrich, Merck, Germany), 1mM sodium orthovanadate (Sigma-Aldrich, Merck, Germany), cOmplete™ Protease Inhibitor Cocktail, PhosSTOP™ (both Roche Diagnostics GmbH, Germany), 250 U ml -1 benzonase (LubioScience GmbH, Switzerland), and 10 U ml -1 DNase I (Roche Diagnostics GmbH, Germany).
Samples were incubated at 4°C for 1 hour and then centrifuged at 13,000xg at 4 °C for 15min.

The supernatant was transferred to a protein LoBind tube (Eppendorf SE, Germany) and the protein concentration was quantified using a commercial bicinchoninic acid assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA).

An amount of 5μg of protein per sample was digested (Trypsin, Promega Corporation, USA) using an AssayMAP Bravo liquid handling system (Agilent Technologies, USA) running the autoSP3 protocol according to Müller et al. (81).

text.text: After sample preparation, the remaining peptides were vacuum dried and stored at -20 °C until LC-MS/MS analysis.
Samples were processed and measured in a block randomized order to prevent any technical bias that might occur during sample preparation or LC-MS/MS measurement (82).
text.formatted: Samples were processed and measured in a block randomized order to prevent any technical bias that might occur during sample preparation or LC-MS/MS measurement <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(82)</ref>.

text.text: Dried peptides were reconstituted (97.4% water, 2.5% hexafluoro-2-propanol and 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid) and 200ng were analysed using a Vanquish Neo UPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) directly connected to an Astral Zoom mass spectrometer for a total of 30 min per sample.

Peptides were online desalted on a trapping cartridge (Acclaim PepMap300 C18, 5µm, 300Å wide pore; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) with a loading volume of 60µL using a 30 µL/min flow of 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in water.

The analytical multistep gradient (400 nL/min) was performed with an Aurora Ultimate XT analytical column (1.7 µm, 75 µm x 250 mm, IonOptics, Australia) using solvent A (0.1% formic acid in water) and solvent B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile).
For 24.5 min the concentration of B linearly ramped from 2% to 30%, followed by a quick ramp to 80%.
Eluting peptides were analyzed in the mass spectrometer using data independent acquisition (DIA) mode.
A full scan at 240k resolution (380-980 m/z, 500% AGC target, 5 ms maxIT) was followed by 300 DIA windows.
The DIA acquisition covered a mass range of 380-980 m/z using windows of fixed width.
Windows overlap by 2 m/z, the AGC target was 100% with a maxIT of 3 ms and spectra are recorded using Astral analyser.
All laboratory technicians performing the measurement were blinded to the clinical data and group allocation.
The normalized data derived from Spectronaut was screened for gene name duplicates.
Only the event with the highest number of identified precursors across all samples was kept.
The dataset was then filtered for proteins that were quantified in ≥70% of the samples in at least one group × time point combination.
Following log2 transformation, missing values were imputed separately within each group-by-timepoint combination using the missForest package (84).

text.text: Data distribution was assessed for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test and checked for linearity via quantile-quantile plots and histograms.
In case of normal distribution, group differences were assessed using two-sided unpaired Student´s t-tests, otherwise the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test was applied.
The level of significance was set at p ≤ 0.05.
Effect sizes were calculated using the effectsize package (89), with Cohen's d (d) reported for parametric comparisons and the rank-biserial correlation (rrb) for nonparametric comparisons.

Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to assess associations between continuous variables, whereas Spearman's rank correlation coefficient was used when at least one variable was ordinal (i.e., EDSS).
Correlation coefficients are reported together with the corresponding two-sided p-values.

For the exploratory correlation matrix comprising multiple pairwise comparisons (Fig. 5C), pvalues were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR).

Group (intervention, passive control), time point (baseline, postintervention, follow-up), and their interaction (group × time) were included as fixed effects, while subject ID was included as a random intercept and the baseline value as a fixed covariate (90).

text.text: The significance of the fixed effects (group, time point, and interaction) was then assessed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) via the built-in anova function from R stats.

Statistical significance was defined as an adjusted two-sided p-value of ≤ 0.05.

Effect sizes (Cohen's d) for significant pairwise comparisons (group and time) were calculated from the estimated marginal means using the residual standard deviation of the mixed model with the eff_size function from the emmeans package (93).

text.text: To identify proteins that are significantly altered between the intervention and passive control group, linear models were fitted to log2-transformed, normalized, and imputed protein intensities using the limma R package (94).
To account for repeated measurements, within-subject correlation was estimated using the duplicateCorrelation function with subject ID as the blocking factor.
The model included the group (intervention, passive control), the time point (baseline, post-intervention, follow-up), and their interaction (group × time) as fixed factors.

Moderated t-statistics (95) were computed for each predefined contrast using the empirical Bayes approach implemented in the eBayes function with mean-variance trend correction and robust variance estimation.

Resulting p-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (92) to control the FDR, and statistical significance was defined as an adjusted two-sided pvalue of ≤ 0.05.

Empirical Bayes moderation was applied using the eBayes function, and predefined contrasts were used to assess within-group temporal changes and group × time interactions.

Resulting p-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (92) to control the FDR, and statistical significance was defined as an adjusted two-sided p-value of ≤ 0.05.

Inter-individual variability was calculated as the coefficient of variation (CV) for each protein across all participants separated by group allocation (intervention, passive control) and time point (pre, post-intervention, follow-up) using non-log2 transformed, non-imputed, filtered data to avoid potential bias arising from imputation and data incompleteness.

Exercise-induced effects on cellular inflammation indices and T cell activity of several TFs was modulated in the intervention group over time with the strongest repressive effect observed for STAT1 activity (p = 2.0×10 -2 , log2FC = -0.170) (Fig.4C), thereby contrasting the results observed in the passive control group.

An exercise-induced modulatory effect on CD4 + T cell differentiation was suggested by a decrease in GATA3 activity (p = 4.4×10 -2 , log2FC = -0.071), the master transcription factor of TH2 cells, or an increase in NR2F6 activity (p = 2.0×10 -2 , log2FC = 0.096) which has been shown to counteract TFH cell differentiation(40).

text.text: The increased activity of JunB (p = 2.0×10 -2 , log2FC = 0.115) can be linked to enhanced Treg differentiation(41, 42), although experimental evidence from other studies indicate TH17-promoting effects (43), suggesting context-dependent effects that determine downstream JunB signaling.

text.text: The increases in KLF9 (p = 2.0×10 -2 , log2FC = 0.113) and MAFB activity (p = 2.4×10 -2 , log2FC = 0.114) were consistent with the aforementioned observations as KLF9 inhibits STAT1 transcription and enhances M2 macrophage polarization (49), while MAFB contributes to an antiinflammatory profile of monocyte-derived macrophages (50).

On the other hand, an increase in RELA activity (p = 2.4×10 -2 , log2FC = 0.105), a canonical NF-κB subunit and important for TH17 polarization and cytokine production in MS (51), implies an adverse effect on immune cell signaling in response to exercise.

Targeted analysis of proteins involved in the NF-κB signaling pathways showed that the expression of RELA itself and other relevant proteins (i.e., NFKB1, NFKB2) remained mainly unchanged over time and between groups (Fig.4D, Supplementary Fig.S5A).

In contrast, the abundance of STAT1 significantly decreased from pre-intervention to follow-up in the intervention group and was complemented by similar kinetics for STAT2, STAT6, and other related proteins (Fig.4D, Supplementary Fig.S5B) which underlines the finding of a decrease in inferred STAT1 activity.
Interestingly, CLOCK activity was significantly reduced at follow-up in the intervention group compared to the passive control group (p = 2.6×10 -2 , log2FC = -0.164) (Fig.4C).

Besides being a core component of the transcriptional circadian clock machinery, CLOCK is implicated in the activation of NF-κB (52) and the NLRP3 inflammasome (53) which contrasts the finding of increased RELA activity (p = 3.7×10 -2 , log2FC = 0.156) in the intervention group.

Although enhanced NR2F6 (p = 2.6×10 -2 , log2FC = 0.137) and decreased MAZ (p = 2.1×10 -2 , log2FC = -0.122) activities in the intervention group compared to the passive control group indicate a reduced STAT1 signaling and an attenuated induction of TFH differentiation(38, 40), a decreased BACH2 activity (p = 2.1×10 -2 , log2FC = -0.141) implicates a diminished ability to stabilize Treg function and to repress TH17-mediated inflammatory signaling(54, 55).

Using state-of-the-art UHPLC-MS/MS-based analysis of the PBMC proteome, we identified considerably more differentially abundant proteins at follow-up compared to post-intervention with most of them being decreased in the intervention group.

This suggests that a recovery period with reduced cardiovascular and musculoskeletal strain may be necessary for (delayed) proteomic and immunometabolic adaptations to emerge in circulating immune cells in response to training.

Our findings point to an altered mitochondrial metabolism indicative of a diminished mitochondrial respiration or a reduced synthesis of macromolecules, lipids, and nucleotides that leads to an attenuated proliferation of immune cells(63), a mode of action of some DMTs (e.g., teriflunomide or cladribine).

text.text: Taken together, most changes in the PBMC proteome indicate a shift toward an anti-inflammatory state both on the protein and inferred TF activity level, although some results suggest a more complex or partially divergent response.

Since the results on transcriptional regulation were based on inferential TF activity modelling and reflect changes in the abundance of proteins encoded by downstream TF target genes, future studies should elaborate on these findings by validating an activation or inhibition of highlighted TF as well as associated signaling pathways.

The rating of perceived exertion (RPE, Borg scale (6-20)) (76) was recorded every three minutes (min) and immediately after exercise cessation.
The highest 15 seconds interval during the CPET was used to calculate V ̇O2peak and PPO values.
In brief, male and female participants conducted a steep ramp test after a calibration phase of 1 min and a warm-up phase of 2 min at 25 watts (W) for females and 50 W for males, respectively.

Based on the participants BMI and the metabolic equivalent score, retrieved from the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire (GPAQ) questionnaire (77), a ramp protocol was chosen to increase either 10 or 15 W/min for females and 15 or 20 W/min for males, respectively.

Physical activity and sleep behavior was monitored for seven days by a wearable device (ActiGraph TM , Pensacola, USA) after baseline testing and before study commencement (week 0), in week 6 of the intervention phase, and in the weeks after the intervention phase (week 13) and follow-up (week 17), respectively.
cytometry analysis was performed using a Cytek® Northern Lights™ full spectrum flow cytometer (Cytek Biosciences, California, USA).

Cryopreserved PBMCs were gently thawed in a water bath at 37°C with a mean recovery across all groups and time points of 90.5 ± 4.8% viable cells assessed with the Zombie NIR™ Fixable Viability Kit (BioLegend, San Diego, CA, USA).
In brief, 1x10 6 PBMCs were incubated with a master mix containing Brilliant Stain buffer (BD Biosciences) and antibodies against surface antigens for 30 min at 4°C in the dark.

The antibody cocktail comprised anti-CD20 (BV421, clone 2H7), anti-CD3 (Alexa Fluor 700, clone SK7), anti-CD45RA (BV570, clone HI100), anti-CD49d (BV510, clone 9F10), anti-CD62L (BV711, clone DREG-56), anti-CD69 (BV605, clone FN50), anti-CD279 (APC, clone NAT105), anti-CX3CR1 (PE-CF594, clone 2A9-1), anti-CD196 (BV785, clone G034E3), anti-CD194 (PerCP/Fire 806, clone L291H4), anti-CD183 (APC/Fire 810, clone G025H7), anti-CD165 (APC/Fire 750, clone KPL-1) (all from BioLegend, San Diego, CA, USA), anti-CD4 (PerCP, clone SK3), anti-CD8 (BV750, clone SK1), anti-CD25 (BB700, clone M-A251), anti-LFA-1α (BV480, clone G43-25B), anti-CD185 (BB515, clone RF8B2), anti-CD186 (RB744, clone 13B 1E5) (all from BD Biosciences, NJ, USA) and anti-CD56 (violetFluor450, clone MY31) (Cytek Biosciences).

After washing, cells were fixed for 40 min at 4°C in the dark using the BD Pharmingen™ Fixation Buffer and then incubated with BD Pharmingen™ permeabilization buffer and anti-Ki-67 (Alexa Fluor 647, clone Ki-67), and anti-Foxp3 (PE, clone 259D/C7) for intracellular staining for 45 min at 4°C in the dark.
Cells were acquired on the flow cytometer within two hours after finishing the staining protocol.
Gating was performed using FlowJo™ 10.10.1 (see Supplementary Fig S3 for gating strategy).

Tregs were phenotyped as CD4 + Foxp3 + CD25 high , TH1 cells as CD4 + CXCR3 + CCR4 -CCR6 -, TH2 cells as CD4 + CXCR3 -CCR4 + CCR6 -, TH17 cells as CD4 + CXCR3 -CCR4 + CCR6 + , TH17.1 cells as CD4 + CXCR3 + CCR4 -CCR6 + , and TFH cells as CD4 + CXCR5 + .
Monocytes were identified based on SSC and FSC parameters.
Mean fluorescence intensity (MFI), quantified as the geometric mean, was calculated in FlowJo™ and used as a relative surrogate marker of the cell´s protein expression level.
Analysis of DIA RAW files was performed with Spectronaut (Biognosys, version 21.0.260703.94842, settings profile 2024-09-03_LFQ_MS) (83) in directDIA+ (Deep) library free mode.
Default settings were applied with the following relevant parameters.

Within DIA Analysis under Identification, the Precursor Qvalue Cutoff and Precursor PEP Cutoff were set to 0.01, and Protein Qvalue Cutoff (Run and Experiment) as well as Protein PEP Cutoff were set to 0.01; Run level protein scoring used the "Highest Scoring Observation (SN19 default)" rule.
In Quantification, the Proteotypicity Filter was set to "Only Protein Group Specific", the Protein LFQ Method was set to MaxLFQ and the Quantification window was set to "Not Synchronized (SN 17)".
In Post Analysis, "Use All MS Level Quantities" was set to True.

The data were searched against the human reference proteome from UniProt (one protein sequence per gene; 20,659 entries, FASTA dated 29 th January 2026) and a contaminants FASTA (246 unique entries from 12 th of June 2025), and experimental conditions were included in the Spectronaut setup.
